The Axiom of Choice

Pick one dot from each row of a table. See why finite collections and infinite ones differ.

The question is whether picking can be made into a function. Finitely many sets: just pick, one by one. Infinitely many: the picking rule itself needs a guarantee. That guarantee is the axiom of choice.

For example, every 📦 box holds some 🍬 candies. With three boxes, just reach in and pick. With endless boxes, you need the rule 'one from each box'. Nobody can check them all by eye.

Prove no axiom is needed for a finite family: if X1,…,XmX_1, \dots, X_mX1​,…,Xm​ are all nonempty sets, there exists a tuple (x1,…,xm)(x_1, \dots, x_m)(x1​,…,xm​) picking one element from each XiX_iXi​ (induction on mmm).

X1,…,Xm≠∅ ⇒ ∃ (x1,…,xm):xi∈XiX_1, \dots, X_m \ne \varnothing \ \Rightarrow\ \exists\,(x_1, \dots, x_m): x_i \in X_iX1​,…,Xm​=∅ ⇒ ∃(x1​,…,xm​):xi​∈Xi​
Show proof

  2. Inductive step: suppose a tuple (x1,…,xm)(x_1, \dots, x_m)(x1​,…,xm​) has already been picked from X1,…,XmX_1, \dots, X_mX1​,…,Xm​ (xi∈Xix_i \in X_ixi​∈Xi​). Since Xm+1≠∅X_{m+1} \ne \varnothingXm+1​=∅, some xm+1∈Xm+1x_{m+1} \in X_{m+1}xm+1​∈Xm+1​ exists, and (x1,…,xm,xm+1)(x_1, \dots, x_m, x_{m+1})(x1​,…,xm​,xm+1​) is a tuple for the m+1m+1m+1 sets.

  3. Hence a tuple exists for every finite mmm.

    The point: at each step we pick from a single named set — never "simultaneously" from infinitely many sets — so no choice axiom is needed.

    For an infinite family this induction never finishes, and that is exactly where the axiom enters.

Prove in both directions that the axiom of choice is equivalent to "every product of nonempty sets is nonempty".

AC  ⟺  (Xi≠∅ ∀i ⇒ ∏i∈IXi≠∅)\mathrm{AC} \iff \left( X_i \ne \varnothing\ \forall i \ \Rightarrow\ \prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \varnothing \right)AC⟺(Xi​=∅ ∀i ⇒ i∈I∏​Xi​=∅)
Show proof

  1. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) Assume AC, and take a family (Xi)i∈I(X_i)_{i \in I}(Xi​)i∈I​ of nonempty sets.

    The axiom gives a choice function ccc with c(i)∈Xic(i) \in X_ic(i)∈Xi​ for each iii.

  2. (⇐\Leftarrow⇐) Conversely, assume every such product is nonempty.

Prove in both directions that the axiom of choice is equivalent to "every surjection has a right inverse".

Show proof
